item.description:
**⌘W closes the tab again, not the window.** Since 0.1.3, ⌘W went to the system's own Close rather than Shellhand's Close Tab, so it closed the whole window. With a session still running it asked about the window; with nothing running it closed the window and every tab in it without a word. ⌘W closes the tab in front again, asking first while its session is still running, and closes SFTP or Settings when one of them is in front.
**A session that is still connecting says so.** A warning ssh prints before it reaches the host — a key file that is not there is the usual one — made the session read as connected: its tab went green and Stop Connecting greyed out while ssh was still trying. Those warnings no longer count as the host answering, so the session stays connecting, with its time and Stop Connecting, until something does.
**Show Beside fits the window.** Showing a tab beside the one in front widened the window past the edge of the screen, cutting off the right-hand side and pushing the inspector out of reach. The two sides now share the width the window has, half each to begin with, and the line between them can be dragged.
**An import leaves your hosts where you filed them.** The group typed into "Put new hosts in" was given to every host the file left unfiled, including ones already in your list, so importing your ssh config a second time with a group typed moved hosts out of the groups you had put them in. It now files only the hosts the import adds.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 746 checks to 753. A walk through the whole window after 0.1.4 found all four of these, and the window check now fails if ⌘W belongs to anything but Close Tab.

**Renaming a host takes what goes through it along.** A host that others jumped through, named in their Through field or in a group's, left them naming a machine no longer in the list once it was renamed, and ssh was left to find one by that name on its own. Saving a new name now rewrites every host's and group's Through field that named the old one, and the editor says what will follow before you save — "6 hosts and the groups EU and US go through bastion, and will follow the new name."
**The window opens with the keyboard in the host list.** macOS gave it to the search field, the window's first text field, so ↓ and Return did nothing until the list was clicked. Now the arrows walk the list and Return connects from the moment the window opens. ⌘F still goes to the search.
**A host called bastion is no longer offered itself to jump through.** The Through field's grey example was "bastion" on every host, which on a host called bastion read as the loop Shellhand refuses to save. There it suggests "gateway" instead.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 737 checks to 746, and the README's picture and shellhand.com show the window as it is now, where they showed an older one.

**A session says what it is doing while it connects.** A tab that is connecting shows where it is going, the way there and how long it has taken — "deploy@192.0.2.21:2222, through bastion · 4 s" — with Stop Connecting beside it, and on ⌘. in the Terminal menu, where the only way out was closing the tab.
**An ending says what happened, in words.** A session that finishes says whether it couldn't connect, lost its connection, was stopped, or simply ended. Up to 0.1.2 "status 255" read the same as typing `exit`. ssh's last line is shown, with what it means under it for somebody who did not write ssh: a name this Mac can't look up, a machine that answered with nothing listening, a key the machine turned down, a key that has changed. Reconnecting keeps the tab where it was in the strip, where it used to close it and open another at the end.
**A new machine's key is asked about by name.** The first time ssh meets a machine, the question comes up in a sheet over its tab, saying which machine it is, where it sits on the way to the host you asked for, and its fingerprint. Return trusts it and Esc does not. A question in a tab behind another marks that tab Needs you, since ssh gives up on a question left unanswered too long.
**A tab shows its state as a symbol and says it in words**, under the window's title, where a colour alone said it to nobody who cannot tell red from green.
**SFTP says why it cannot open a host, and what to do about it.** A key that has changed, a machine never connected to, a host that takes only a password, a key the host turned down: each is said as itself. Where a terminal can do what SFTP cannot — answer ssh's question about a new machine's key, or type a password — Open in Terminal opens a tab on that host. Every failure offers Try Again.
**The SFTP window answers to its keys.** ⌘R refreshes the side you are working in and ⇧⌘N makes a folder there. Space opens Quick Look, ⌫ deletes, and a folder can be renamed as a file can. The host menu is in order.
**A transfer says which way it goes.** Each row in the strip says where it comes from and where it lands — "This Mac → web-us-1:/var/www/site" — and a failed one can be retried in its own row while the connections it went through are still open. Opening a folder clears what was selected in the one before. One file is "1 item", not "1 items". A finished transfer's bar is drawn full.
**A palette is chosen by looking at it, everywhere.** The inspector, the host and group editors and Settings ▸ Terminal all open the same picker, which draws each palette in its own colours and applies a choice at once, so two can be compared on the terminal behind it. Three of the four were a menu of names. What a host inherits is named for what it inherits — "From Production — Gruvbox Dark".
**Import brings in what it showed you.** A path changed and Returned, or a group typed after the preview, used to import a file or into a group nobody had looked at, and a second press reported the first one's count. The import now runs on exactly what was previewed. The preview says what it would do — "Would add 5 and update 2 · 3 already here" — and a file that isn't there is said as one.
**The settings file has one name, and Settings can make it.** Settings ▸ General ▸ Where things are names it, with Create Settings File, which writes one with every setting explained and commented out — never over a file already there. Once it exists, the button opens it. It was called three different things, and nothing made it.
**Deleting says what else goes.** Deleting a host that others jump through says how many hosts reach their machines through it and which groups name it, and that without it ssh is left to find a machine by that name on its own. Deleting a tag asks first, with the number of hosts it comes off, where it went from all of them without a word.
**⌘F finds hosts.** With the host list in front, ⌘F puts the keyboard in the sidebar's search field, bringing the sidebar back if it was hidden; with a session in front it still searches the terminal. Quick Connect wears a bolt in the toolbar, rather than the magnifying glass the search field under it already wears. The tags under the sidebar wrap onto another line instead of running off its edge. With nothing open there is no strip holding a lone Hosts tab.
**⌘W closes Settings and the SFTP window**, where it did nothing.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 677 checks to 737, and every change was driven on screen against a copy of the app with a host list of its own. That is how the delete warning was found saying "the jump host for 2 groups" about a machine six hosts go through.
